transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, thank you for seeing me. Honestly, what brings me in is... well, it’s my head. It just feels so terribly cloudy lately, like there's a thick fog in there. I manage community associations—HOAs, condo buildings, that sort of thing—and I’ve been doing it a long time. I’m 64, and I’ve always prided myself on being sharp, especially since I had to work my way up from the bottom, not having gone past the eighth grade, you know? You have to be quick on your feet in this business to keep the residents happy. 

But lately... I don't know, I'll be sitting at my desk, and I just stare at a board packet. Just stare right at the pages. Or I’ll get a vendor email—like the other day, the landscaping company emailed asking if we wanted the winter mulch put down on Tuesday or Thursday, which is a nothing question, right?—and I just cannot decide. I mean, these are simple, everyday things! I used to handle them so fast, just boom, boom, boom, reply sent, problem solved, moving on to the next property. But now, it’s like my brain just stalls out. I’ll read the same sentence from a vendor over and over, and I just sit there with this cloudy feeling, completely unable to make a basic choice about mulch or gate repairs or whatever it is, and before I know it I've wasted an hour just trying to answer one simple question...
Have you been feeling sad or down lately?

Sad? Hmm. You know, it's funny you ask that, because my sister was just asking me the exact same thing on Sunday. She calls me every Sunday morning, regular as clockwork, right after she gets back from her church service down in Florida, and she told me I sounded really down. But I had to think about it, and I told her that I really do not think I am sad. I am really not. It is not like I am sitting around crying or feeling sorry for myself, you know? I have never been the type to just sit and weep. Even back when things were really tough, when I was first starting out in the property business and trying to make a name for myself without a high school diploma, I never let myself get down in the dumps. I just kept pushing. 

So no, I don't have that heavy, crying kind of feeling at all. It is really just that fog I was telling you about. It is like... I am not sad about the landscaping email, I just literally cannot process it. I just feel sort of blank. Not sad, just completely stalled out. Like a car engine that just will not turn over, but the car itself isn't crying or upset, if that makes sense. It just sits there in the driveway. So I wouldn't use the word sad for how I've been feeling, no.
Have you been feeling anxious or nervous lately?

Anxious? Well... no, not really. I mean, I'm not sitting around worrying about things, if that's what you mean. I'm not pacing the floors or biting my nails or anything like that. I've never been a nervous person. You can't be in my line of work. When you're managing a hundred-unit condo building and the boiler goes out on Christmas Eve—which happened to me back in 2018, let me tell you, that was a nightmare—you can't panic. You have to just get on the phone, call the emergency HVAC guys, deal with the board president who's yelling because his in-laws are visiting and it's freezing... you just handle it. You can't be anxious. 

And even now, with this... this cloudiness in my head, I'm not nervous about it. I'm frustrated, absolutely. It's incredibly frustrating to just sit there staring at a simple email about pool maintenance and not be able to formulate a reply. But I don't feel that tight, nervous feeling in my chest or anything. I'm not having panic attacks. It's just... nothing. Just a blank wall. So no, I wouldn't say I'm anxious or nervous at all, really. Just stuck.
Have you been having any trouble sleeping lately?

Sleep? No, my sleep is completely fine. I've always been a good sleeper, honestly. You have to be in this business, you really need your rest to deal with people all day. I usually turn in around 10:30, right after I watch the local news. I always like to see what the weather's going to be like because, you know, if there's a freeze warning or heavy rain coming, I have to make sure the maintenance guys are prepped for the older properties. The townhomes over on Elm Street, for instance, their gutters always overflow if we get more than an inch of rain, so I have to stay on top of that. 

But anyway, I watch the news, I turn off the TV, and I am out like a light. Always have been. And I sleep right through until about 5:30 or 6:00 in the morning, regular as a metronome. I don't toss and turn, I don't wake up in the middle of the night staring at the ceiling or anything like that. I just sleep. 

And you know, you'd think that getting a good, solid seven or eight hours would help with that cloudy feeling in my head I was telling you about, but it doesn't make a lick of difference. I wake up, I feel perfectly rested in my body, I go to the kitchen and make my coffee—just black, I don't mess with all that cream and sugar nonsense—and I sit down at my computer to start the day, and... the fog is just still right there waiting for me. So the sleep itself is perfectly fine, I don't have any trouble dropping off or staying asleep at all, it's just that sleeping doesn't seem to fix whatever is going on with my brain during the day.
Have you been having any trouble remembering things lately?

Memory? Well, let me think about that. I wouldn't call it a memory problem, exactly, no. I mean, I know what day it is, I know all my tenants' names, I remember exactly what we paid for snow removal back in the winter of 2015 when we had that massive blizzard. I've got a mind like a steel trap for numbers and dates, always have, even without much formal schooling. You learn to keep it all up here when you're managing multiple properties, you know? You have to remember who is in arrears, who has a dog they aren't supposed to have, all of it. 

But... and this is really the whole reason I made the appointment to come see you in the first place... it's not the remembering, it's the thinking part. My head just feels so incredibly cloudy. It's exactly like I was saying before with that fog. I will sit down at my desk and pull up a board packet for one of the upcoming condo association meetings, or open up a vendor email—like that landscaping quote I mentioned—and I just stare at it. I stare and I stare. And I cannot decide what to do with it. 

These are simple things, Doctor. Things I used to handle so fast you wouldn't believe it. I'd look at a quote, check the budget in my head, and boom, boom, boom—approved, denied, or I'd get on the phone and negotiate them down ten percent. I used to fly through my inbox before 9:00 AM. And now? Now I just sit there looking at a basic email about, I don't know, replacing the lobby mats for the winter season, and I can't make a simple decision. My brain just refuses to process it. It's like wading through thick mud. So I remember the email is there, and I remember what a lobby mat is, I just can't seem to think my way through it to actually do my job anymore.
Do you ever find yourself struggling to find the right words when you're trying to explain something or respond to someone?

Finding the right words? No, no, I don't have any trouble with that. If I need to tell somebody something, I know exactly what to say. Just the other day, I had to talk to Mrs. Gable over in unit 4B. She's been sneaking her sister's cat in, and I had to lay it out for her. I told her plain as day that the bylaws are the bylaws, and we agreed to no pets on the fourth floor because of Mr. Henderson's allergies right across the hall. I didn't stumble over my words at all. I never do. I've always been a straight shooter, you know? 

If somebody is standing right in front of me, or if I'm on the phone with the plumbers—like when the main line backed up at the Oakwood property last spring, oh what a terrible mess that was, raw sewage all over the communal laundry room, I had to get the specialty cleaners out there and everything—I can talk their ear off and tell them exactly what needs doing. The words are all right there in my head, lined up and ready to go. I don't lose my train of thought or forget what a thing is called. I can explain things just fine. 

It's just... like I was trying to explain before, it's that awful mud in my brain when I have to sit down by myself and process the paperwork or make a choice. But the actual talking? Communicating with people? No, talking has never been a problem for me. The words come just as easy as they always have. I just don't always know what decision I'm supposed to be making with them lately.
Have you been having trouble planning out your day or organizing your tasks lately?

Planning my day? Oh, heavens no. I am as organized as they come. You have to be, you know. When you manage as many units as I do, if you don't have a solid plan, you are just dead in the water. I have my whole week laid out on this big desk calendar. I still use the paper ones, the big blotters? I like to physically write it all down. 

Mondays are for the townhomes, checking the grounds, making sure the trash was picked up properly because sometimes those municipal trucks just blow right past the dumpsters in the back alley if the cars are parked too close. Tuesdays are my vendor days, Wednesdays are for the condo board prep... I have a system, and it works. I even make a list every single evening before I leave the office so I know exactly what I'm walking into the next morning. Number one, call the roofer about the flashing on unit 12. Number two, follow up on the late fees for the Smithson brothers. They're always late, those two, nice boys but they just can't seem to get a check in the mail by the first of the month to save their lives. 

So the organizing part, the knowing what my day is supposed to look like and what tasks need doing? That's perfectly fine. My schedule is practically ironclad. I've got color-coded folders for every property, for crying out loud. It's just... well, it goes right back to what I keep saying. It's when I actually sit down to *do* the things on the list that require me to think and make a choice. The list is right there. The plan is right there. I know I'm supposed to review the roofing bids at 10:00 AM. But then 10:00 AM rolls around, I open the folder, and I just sit and stare at the numbers through that awful fog. 

But no, the organizing itself is second nature to me. I've been doing it for thirty years, long before they had all these fancy computer programs to do it for you. I could plan out a property maintenance schedule in my sleep! So that's definitely not the problem.
Do you find it hard to focus on a single task for an extended period of time?

Focus? Well, it really depends on what you mean by focus. If you mean, do I get distracted and wander off to go water the office plants or make a cup of coffee every five minutes? No, not at all. I can sit at my desk and look at one single piece of paper for an hour straight. 

But... well, that's exactly what I keep coming back to, Doctor. That is the entire reason what brings me in today. I can focus my eyes on something, sure, but my head just feels so incredibly cloudy that all that focus doesn't actually do me any good. 

Like I was saying before, I will literally just sit there and stare at a board packet. Or I'll open up a vendor email—say, from the landscaping company wanting to know if we're doing the premium dyed mulch or the standard cedar bark this spring, which usually takes me two seconds to answer because I know the operating budget for that property inside and out—and I just stare at the screen. I am completely focused on it, but I cannot decide even simple things that I used to handle so fast. I just sit there looking at the words, trapped in that awful fog, completely unable to make a choice. 

So, yes, I suppose I stay on that one single task for a very extended period of time, but I don't actually get anywhere with it! I just spin my wheels. Do you see what I mean? It's not that my attention is jumping all over the place, it's just this heavy cloud in my head that absolutely refuses to let me process the thing I'm focusing on.
Do you find yourself feeling indifferent or unmotivated about things that you used to care about?

Well, yes, actually. That's... that's another thing that's been bothering me so much lately. It's not just the work and the paperwork and the fog, it's... it's my whole life outside the office, too. I just don't have the drive for any of it anymore. 

Take my dance class, for instance. I've been going to this lovely little ballroom and Latin dance class at the community center for, oh, it must be five years now. We have such a wonderful time, a whole group of us ladies, and sometimes a few gentlemen join in. We were learning the rumba last month, and usually, I would be practicing my steps in the kitchen while I wait for the kettle to boil. But lately? The thought of going just feels like... like trying to walk through wet cement. I haven't gone in three weeks. I just sit in my armchair and let the evening pass. 

And it's the same with the weekend art galleries. I've always loved strolling down Main Street on a Saturday afternoon, popping into the little galleries, seeing what the local watercolor artists are up to. I bought a beautiful piece last year, a landscape of the old mill downtown, but now... I just don't care. I don't care what they're hanging on the walls. The idea of getting dressed and walking down there just seems so pointless. 

Even Sunday dinners... oh, that breaks my heart the most. I have always, always cooked a big Sunday dinner for my family. A proper roast, usually, with the potatoes and the carrots and a nice gravy from scratch. My grandchildren love my Yorkshire puddings. It's the highlight of my week, having them all around the big oak table, laughing and passing the serving dishes. But the last two Sundays, I just couldn't bring myself to do it. I told them I wasn't feeling up to it and we ordered pizzas instead. Pizzas! On a Sunday! It just doesn't feel right. Those are the things that usually make me feel like *me*, you know? The dancing, the art, feeding my family... and right now, I just feel completely indifferent to all of it. I just don't want to do any of it.
Do you feel like you've lost interest in activities that you normally enjoy?

Well, yes, Doctor, that is exactly what I was just telling you! It’s like we’re on the exact same wavelength here. But yes, absolutely, one hundred percent. Like I was just saying, I have not wanted to go to my dance class, or look at the little galleries, or cook the Sunday food for my family... I just haven't wanted to do a single bit of it. 

And I keep bringing it up because it really upsets me, to be honest with you. Those are the things that usually make me feel like myself. If I'm not the lady who dances the rumba and makes the best Yorkshire puddings in the neighborhood, then who on earth am I? Just a tired old woman staring at property files all day? 

Usually, I'd be down at the butcher on Thursday morning—I always go to Sal's on 4th Street because he knows exactly how much fat to leave on a roast so it doesn't dry out in the oven—but I haven't even walked past his window in weeks. I just don't have the interest. And the art... I know I already mentioned the watercolors, but it really is so strange for me. I used to know half the local painters by name. Now, if someone came to my door and handed me a free ticket to a grand gallery opening, I’d probably just toss it right into the recycling bin. 

I just sit in my chair and think about how I *should* want to go, how I *should* want to be out there doing the things I love, but the desire is just completely gone. It’s like someone just walked into the room and pulled my plug right out of the wall. So yes, to answer your question, the interest is just completely gone from the things I normally love, and I just don't know how to get it back.
Do you have trouble initiating tasks or projects on your own?

Initiating tasks? Well, no, not really. I mean, I know I just went on and on about the fog in my head and sitting in my chair and not wanting to do my hobbies, but starting things isn't really the issue. 

If I know something has to be done, I'll start it. Like at work, if I get a new property file on my desk, I will physically open the folder. I'll take the papers out. I'll turn on my computer and pull up the spreadsheet. I can initiate the whole process just fine. It's the *doing* of it that gets me stuck, like I said before. I'll get it all laid out in front of me, ready to go, and then I just stare at it because my brain won't make a decision. 

And it's the same at home. If the laundry basket is full, I can pick it up and carry it down to the basement. I can sort the whites from the darks—I always wash my towels separately, of course, because you don't want lint getting all over your nice dark slacks—and I can put them in the machine and turn the dial. Starting the chore isn't the problem. 

It's just that once I've started something, or if it's something that requires me to actually think or care, like the cooking or the dancing, that's where I fall apart. But just initiating a task? No, I can still get the ball rolling, so to speak. It just doesn't roll very far once I push it.
Do you feel like you're just going through the motions of daily life without any real purpose or motivation?

Well, yes, exactly. I feel like I'm just a ghost haunting my own life right now, to be perfectly honest. I know we're sort of circling around the same drain here, and I know I keep harping on this, but it’s because it's the truest way I can explain what's happening to me. 

I get up in the morning, I put on my slacks and a blouse, I make my piece of toast—just plain rye, I don't even bother with the nice marmalade anymore because I don't really care what it tastes like—and I go into the property office. I go through the motions of the day. But there's no spark to any of it. There's no purpose. 

Because the purpose, the real meaning in my week, used to come from all those other things we were just talking about. But I have not wanted to go to my dance class, I haven't wanted to look at the little galleries downtown, and I haven't wanted to cook the Sunday food for my family. And I know I just told you all of that, but you have to understand, those are the things that usually make me feel like *myself*. Without them, who am I? What am I even doing? 

It’s like being on a treadmill. You’re walking and walking, and your legs are moving, and you're doing the things you're supposed to do to get through a Tuesday, but you aren't actually going anywhere beautiful. The dancing, the art, feeding my grandchildren... that was the beautiful part of my life. Now it's just... motions. Just putting one foot in front of the other because I suppose the rent needs paying and the laundry needs doing, but I have absolutely no heart in it anymore. It's just a terribly empty way to live, feeling like a stranger in your own routine.
Do you feel like things that happen to you or around you don't really matter to you anymore?

Well, yes, Doctor, that is exactly it. It’s like a heavy blanket has just been thrown over my whole life, muffling everything. I know I’m sounding like a broken record here, going on and on about the same things, but it’s because it’s so pervasive. Nothing seems to touch me anymore. 

Like I was saying earlier about the dancing and the galleries... I just, I have not wanted to go to my dance class at all. And the little galleries downtown? I used to love strolling past them on a Saturday, seeing what new pieces were up in the windows. Now, I could walk right by and not even turn my head. And the Sunday food for my family... I haven't wanted to cook it. I just haven't. And that’s what I mean when I say things don't matter. Those are the things that usually make me feel like myself! They are the core of who I am. 

If my grandson came over right now and told me he got an A on his spelling test, I know I should feel thrilled. I should want to bake him a batch of my special ginger snaps to celebrate—I always use a little extra molasses because it makes them chewier, you know—but honestly? I think I would just nod and say "that's nice, dear," and go right back to staring at the wall. 

It’s frightening, really, how little I care about the world around me right now. It’s like all the color has been drained out of everything, and I’m just sitting here in black and white, watching it all happen on a screen. The news, the neighbors, my own hobbies... it all just feels so terribly far away and unimportant. So yes, to answer your question, nothing really seems to matter to me at all right now, not even the things that used to matter the most.
Do you feel like you're no longer concerned about things that would normally be important to you?

I know I am just beating a dead horse here, Doctor, and you must be getting so tired of hearing me repeat myself, but yes. That is exactly what I've been trying to say. The things that are normally the most important things in the world to me... I just have absolutely no concern for them right now. 

Take the Sunday food, for instance. Like I said, I haven't wanted to cook it. But normally? Normally, if I didn't have a massive spread on the table by two o'clock on a Sunday, I would be beside myself! I'd be so worried the grandchildren were going hungry, or that my daughter would think I was getting lazy. It was a point of pride, you know? A very important duty for me as a grandmother. But now? The thought of it just makes me tired, and I find I don't even care if they just order a pizza instead. I have no concern for it whatsoever. 

And it is the exact same way with my dance class and looking at the little galleries downtown. I haven't wanted to do any of it, and worse, I'm just not concerned about missing out. Usually I'd be worried about falling behind on the dance steps or letting my partner down, but I just don't care. And like I said before, those are the things that usually make me feel like myself! They are my whole identity outside of the property office. 

To not care about them... to not be concerned that I'm missing weeks of routines or not seeing the new art displays... it's just so strange. It's like my priorities have just completely evaporated into thin air, and I'm left here talking your ear off about it because I don't know how else to explain that the things that make me who I am just don't hold any importance to me right now.
Have you lost a significant amount of weight recently?

Well, I haven't exactly been stepping on the scale, Doctor, because frankly, who wants to do that when they're feeling like this? But my clothes are definitely fitting a bit looser, especially around the waist on those slacks I wear to the property office. 

It's just... my eating has been completely off lately. Completely off. I know I mentioned the plain rye toast earlier, but honestly, most days I don't even finish that. A cup of coffee and maybe a few bites of something dry is enough to carry me through practically the whole day. It's like my stomach has just shrunk, or maybe my brain just forgets that I'm supposed to need fuel to keep going. 

And then, when I finally get home and the day is done, you'd think I'd be ravenous, wouldn't you? But I'm not. I just... I sit there in the kitchen, and I end up just picking at things. I'll pull out a package of flour tortillas—the soft ones, not the corn ones—and I'll just tear off little pieces and eat them plain. Or I'll find some sweets, maybe some stale cookies left over from when the grandkids were here last, and I'll just nibble on those. 

But the thing is, I'm not even really enjoying them. It's not like I'm sitting down to a nice slice of cake and savoring it. It's just mindless picking, like I know I should put something in my stomach but I can't be bothered to actually make a meal or taste what I'm eating. It all just tastes like cardboard anyway. So yes, I suppose I probably have lost some weight, just because I'm practically living on coffee and tortilla scraps, which I know isn't healthy, but I just can't seem to muster the energy to care about food right now.
Do you feel like you're depressed?

Depressed? I... I don't really know if I would use that word. I'm just not sure. You hear people say they're depressed all the time, don't you? Like if it rains on their weekend, or if the grocery store is out of their favorite brand of coffee, or if their television show gets canceled. People throw that word around so much. But this... I don't really know what to call what I'm going through. 

Is that what depression is? Because I'm not sitting around crying all day. If you came to visit me at the property office—I have a nice little desk right near the front window where I can see the main courtyard of the complex—you wouldn't see me weeping over the lease agreements or sobbing into the maintenance requests. I haven't noticed myself feeling terribly sad, exactly. It's more just... well, like I was telling you before with that heavy blanket feeling. It's just an emptiness. 

It's like all the air has been let out of my tires and I'm just riding on the rims, bumping along, waiting for the day to be over. I sit there and look at the clock on the wall and I swear the hands are moving backwards sometimes, just dragging on and on. So, I don't know if the medical books would call me depressed, Doctor. I really couldn't tell you. I just know I feel entirely drained out and disconnected from it all, and I just don't have a proper name for it.
Do you find pleasure in things you used to enjoy?

Well, like I was saying before... I really haven't. It's just so frustrating, Doctor. The things that usually bring me so much joy, the things that make me feel like, well, like *me*... they just don't have any appeal right now. I don't get any spark from them at all. 

I mean, I've already talked your ear off about the Sunday dinners, but that's a perfect example. I used to absolutely love planning the menu, going to the market, getting the freshest ingredients, and spending the whole morning in the kitchen getting everything just right for my daughter and the grandchildren. It was my favorite part of the week! The house would smell so good, and seeing everyone sitting around the table eating what I made... that was my pleasure. But now? I just haven't wanted to cook at all. The thought of it just exhausts me, and there's no joy in it. 

And it's the same with my dance class. I've been going to that class for years. It's a wonderful group of ladies, and we do a little bit of everything—some ballroom, some line dancing, even a little jazz sometimes. It's usually the highlight of my Tuesday and Thursday evenings. I love the music, I love the movement, I love the chatting before and after. But lately... I just haven't wanted to go. I can't find the energy or the desire to put on my dancing shoes. It just feels like a chore instead of something fun. 

Even just taking a stroll downtown to look at the little art galleries... I used to love doing that on a Saturday afternoon. Just wandering in and out, seeing what the local artists have put up, maybe stopping for a cup of tea afterwards. It was so relaxing, so inspiring. But I haven't wanted to do that either. I just sit at home. It's like someone turned down the volume on all the good things in my life, and I just can't find any enjoyment in them anymore. It's a terrible feeling, honestly, to just feel so... flat about the things you usually love.
Do you feel guilty about not being able to enjoy the things you used to?

Well, guilt... yes, I suppose I do feel guilty, but maybe not just about the dinners or the dancing. It's more about my work, Doctor. It really weighs on me. I've been at the property office for a long time, and I know those residents. I know Mrs. Higgins in 4B who needs her handrails checked, and Mr. Abernathy in 2C who's always asking about the landscaping. And lately, I just... I keep thinking about how I've let them down. 

You see, a few months back—well, I don't know exactly when, time just blurs together now—but a while ago, I was feeling so... energized. So full of ideas. I was talking to everyone in the courtyard, telling them we were going to get the fountain fixed, and we were going to put in new patio furniture, and maybe even repaint the common room. I was just talking so big, making all these grand promises to these sweet people who just want a nice place to live. 

And the thing is, I didn't even check the budget. I didn't look at the association's reserve funds or talk to the board before I started going on and on about all these wonderful improvements. I just felt so sure we could do it all, right then and there. And now... now that I'm feeling so drained and empty, I just sit at my desk and look out the window at that broken fountain, and I feel this awful, heavy guilt. 

I feel completely worthless, honestly. Like I'm just a fraud sitting behind that desk. I keep thinking about how disappointed they must be, how I spoke completely out of turn and got their hopes up for nothing. The funny thing is, nobody has actually complained to me. Mrs. Higgins hasn't said a word about the patio furniture, and Mr. Abernathy just waves when he walks by. Nobody has told me I ruined anything or made a mess of it. But I just *know* I did. I can feel it. I let them all down by talking too big and promising things I couldn't deliver, and I just can't shake this feeling that I'm doing a terrible job and failing everyone who relies on me.
Do you find that you no longer derive pleasure from activities that you once found enjoyable?

Well, yes, Doctor, like I was just saying a few minutes ago... it's exactly that. I just don't have the desire to do the things I used to love. It's really quite distressing to me, because those things are what make me feel like, well, like *me*. 

Take my dance class, for instance. I know I mentioned it, but it really used to be the highlight of my week. Tuesday and Thursday evenings, rain or shine, I'd be there with the ladies. We'd do our steps, have a good laugh, maybe complain about our joints a little bit, but it was wonderful. Now, when Tuesday rolls around, I just look at my dancing shoes in the closet and I can't even fathom putting them on. The very thought of trying to keep time with the music or make small talk just feels like climbing a mountain. I haven't wanted to go at all. 

And the galleries downtown... oh, I used to just adore wandering through them on a Saturday. There's this one little place on Main Street that always has the most beautiful watercolors, and I could spend an hour just looking at the brushstrokes and chatting with the owner, Mr. Davies. He always remembers how I like my tea if I stop in the cafe next door. But lately, I haven't even had the slightest urge to go look. I just sit in my chair at home. 

And of course, the Sunday dinners with my family. I've always been the one to cook. It's a tradition! Getting the roast just right, making sure my daughter's favorite potatoes are on the table, seeing the grandchildren's faces when I bring out a pie... that was my joy. That was how I showed them I loved them. But now, I just haven't wanted to cook Sunday food for them at all. The kitchen feels overwhelming, and the joy I used to get from feeding my family is just... gone. It's like all the color has been washed out of my life, Doctor, and I'm just left with this gray, empty feeling where my interests used to be.
Do you feel like you have less energy than you used to?

Energy? Well... no, I wouldn't say that. I know I said a minute ago about not having the energy for my dancing shoes, but I didn't mean it like a physical tiredness, if that makes sense. It's not like my body is worn out or I'm sleeping all day. 

I still get up right at 6:15 every single morning, regular as a clock, just like I have for the last forty years. I make my bed, I fix my coffee—just instant, nothing fancy, I never had the schooling or the money to get into all those expensive machines they have nowadays—and I go straight down to the property office. I'm on my feet plenty, Doctor. Why, just yesterday, I walked the entire perimeter of the complex. That's all six buildings! I had to go check on the gutters behind building C because Mr. Abernathy said they were overflowing into his hydrangeas, and then I walked all the way over to the maintenance shed on the far side of the property to see if the boys had the right ladder to get up there and clean them out. 

So I'm walking, I'm moving around just fine. My body works. I'm not napping in the middle of the afternoon or dragging my feet when I do my rounds. I can still scrub my kitchen floors on my hands and knees, and I do my laundry every Thursday morning like always. The physical energy is absolutely there. doctor.intent: determine the presence of depressed mood
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're depressed?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about depressed mood, but there is no specific symptom for depressed mood (e.g., S024) in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Depressed? I... I don't really know if I would use that word. I'm just not sure. You hear people say they're depressed all the time, don't you? Like if it rains on their weekend, or if the grocery store is out of their favorite brand of coffee, or if their television show gets canceled. People throw that word around so much. But this... I don't really know what to call what I'm going through. 

Is that what depression is? Because I'm not sitting around crying all day. If you came to visit me at the property office—I have a nice little desk right near the front window where I can see the main courtyard of the complex—you wouldn't see me weeping over the lease agreements or sobbing into the maintenance requests. I haven't noticed myself feeling terribly sad, exactly. It's more just... well, like I was telling you before with that heavy blanket feeling. It's just an emptiness. 

It's like all the air has been let out of my tires and I'm just riding on the rims, bumping along, waiting for the day to be over. I sit there and look at the clock on the wall and I swear the hands are moving backwards sometimes, just dragging on and on. So, I don't know if the medical books would call me depressed, Doctor. I really couldn't tell you. I just know I feel entirely drained out and disconnected from it all, and I just don't have a proper name for it.

inference.note: Added more specific depression codes as patient's symptoms align with depression, despite their uncertainty about the term

doctor.question: Do you find pleasure in things you used to enjoy?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Interest
target_item.manifestation: I have not wanted to go to my dance class, look at the little galleries, or cook Sunday food for my family, and those are things that usually make me feel like myself.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about finding pleasure in previously enjoyed activities, which maps directly to the Loss of Interest symptom.

patient.answer:
Well, like I was saying before... I really haven't. It's just so frustrating, Doctor. The things that usually bring me so much joy, the things that make me feel like, well, like *me*... they just don't have any appeal right now. I don't get any spark from them at all. 

I mean, I've already talked your ear off about the Sunday dinners, but that's a perfect example. I used to absolutely love planning the menu, going to the market, getting the freshest ingredients, and spending the whole morning in the kitchen getting everything just right for my daughter and the grandchildren. It was my favorite part of the week! The house would smell so good, and seeing everyone sitting around the table eating what I made... that was my pleasure. But now? I just haven't wanted to cook at all. The thought of it just exhausts me, and there's no joy in it. 

And it's the same with my dance class. I've been going to that class for years. It's a wonderful group of ladies, and we do a little bit of everything—some ballroom, some line dancing, even a little jazz sometimes. It's usually the highlight of my Tuesday and Thursday evenings. I love the music, I love the movement, I love the chatting before and after. But lately... I just haven't wanted to go. I can't find the energy or the desire to put on my dancing shoes. It just feels like a chore instead of something fun. 

Even just taking a stroll downtown to look at the little art galleries... I used to love doing that on a Saturday afternoon. Just wandering in and out, seeing what the local artists have put up, maybe stopping for a cup of tea afterwards. It was so relaxing, so inspiring. But I haven't wanted to do that either. I just sit at home. It's like someone turned down the volume on all the good things in my life, and I just can't find any enjoyment in them anymore. It's a terrible feeling, honestly, to just feel so... flat about the things you usually love.

doctor.intent: Determine the patient's emotional response to their current situation
doctor.question: Do you feel guilty about not being able to enjoy the things you used to?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
target_item.manifestation: I keep thinking I let the residents down by speaking too big and promising things before checking the money, even though nobody has said I ruined anything.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question directly asks about feelings of guilt, which corresponds to the symptom of worthlessness or excessive guilt.

patient.answer:
Well, guilt... yes, I suppose I do feel guilty, but maybe not just about the dinners or the dancing. It's more about my work, Doctor. It really weighs on me. I've been at the property office for a long time, and I know those residents. I know Mrs. Higgins in 4B who needs her handrails checked, and Mr. Abernathy in 2C who's always asking about the landscaping. And lately, I just... I keep thinking about how I've let them down. 

You see, a few months back—well, I don't know exactly when, time just blurs together now—but a while ago, I was feeling so... energized. So full of ideas. I was talking to everyone in the courtyard, telling them we were going to get the fountain fixed, and we were going to put in new patio furniture, and maybe even repaint the common room. I was just talking so big, making all these grand promises to these sweet people who just want a nice place to live. 

And the thing is, I didn't even check the budget. I didn't look at the association's reserve funds or talk to the board before I started going on and on about all these wonderful improvements. I just felt so sure we could do it all, right then and there. And now... now that I'm feeling so drained and empty, I just sit at my desk and look out the window at that broken fountain, and I feel this awful, heavy guilt. 

I feel completely worthless, honestly. Like I'm just a fraud sitting behind that desk. I keep thinking about how disappointed they must be, how I spoke completely out of turn and got their hopes up for nothing. The funny thing is, nobody has actually complained to me. Mrs. Higgins hasn't said a word about the patio furniture, and Mr. Abernathy just waves when he walks by. Nobody has told me I ruined anything or made a mess of it. But I just *know* I did. I can feel it. I let them all down by talking too big and promising things I couldn't deliver, and I just can't shake this feeling that I'm doing a terrible job and failing everyone who relies on me.

doctor.question: Do you find that you no longer derive pleasure from activities that you once found enjoyable?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Interest
target_item.manifestation: I have not wanted to go to my dance class, look at the little galleries, or cook Sunday food for my family, and those are things that usually make me feel like myself.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking again if I have lost pleasure in activities I used to enjoy, which maps directly to the loss of interest symptom.

patient.answer:
Well, yes, Doctor, like I was just saying a few minutes ago... it's exactly that. I just don't have the desire to do the things I used to love. It's really quite distressing to me, because those things are what make me feel like, well, like *me*. 

Take my dance class, for instance. I know I mentioned it, but it really used to be the highlight of my week. Tuesday and Thursday evenings, rain or shine, I'd be there with the ladies. We'd do our steps, have a good laugh, maybe complain about our joints a little bit, but it was wonderful. Now, when Tuesday rolls around, I just look at my dancing shoes in the closet and I can't even fathom putting them on. The very thought of trying to keep time with the music or make small talk just feels like climbing a mountain. I haven't wanted to go at all. 

And the galleries downtown... oh, I used to just adore wandering through them on a Saturday. There's this one little place on Main Street that always has the most beautiful watercolors, and I could spend an hour just looking at the brushstrokes and chatting with the owner, Mr. Davies. He always remembers how I like my tea if I stop in the cafe next door. But lately, I haven't even had the slightest urge to go look. I just sit in my chair at home. 

And of course, the Sunday dinners with my family. I've always been the one to cook. It's a tradition! Getting the roast just right, making sure my daughter's favorite potatoes are on the table, seeing the grandchildren's faces when I bring out a pie... that was my joy. That was how I showed them I loved them. But now, I just haven't wanted to cook Sunday food for them at all. The kitchen feels overwhelming, and the joy I used to get from feeding my family is just... gone. It's like all the color has been washed out of my life, Doctor, and I'm just left with this gray, empty feeling where my interests used to be.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a loss of energy
doctor.question: Do you feel like you have less energy than you used to?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about fatigue or loss of energy, which is a distinct symptom not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Energy? Well... no, I wouldn't say that. I know I said a minute ago about not having the energy for my dancing shoes, but I didn't mean it like a physical tiredness, if that makes sense. It's not like my body is worn out or I'm sleeping all day. 

I still get up right at 6:15 every single morning, regular as a clock, just like I have for the last forty years. I make my bed, I fix my coffee—just instant, nothing fancy, I never had the schooling or the money to get into all those expensive machines they have nowadays—and I go straight down to the property office. I'm on my feet plenty, Doctor. Why, just yesterday, I walked the entire perimeter of the complex. That's all six buildings! I had to go check on the gutters behind building C because Mr. Abernathy said they were overflowing into his hydrangeas, and then I walked all the way over to the maintenance shed on the far side of the property to see if the boys had the right ladder to get up there and clean them out. 

So I'm walking, I'm moving around just fine. My body works. I'm not napping in the middle of the afternoon or dragging my feet when I do my rounds. I can still scrub my kitchen floors on my hands and knees, and I do my laundry every Thursday morning like always. The physical energy is absolutely there. I *could* physically walk down to the art gallery, or I *could* stand at the stove and chop carrots and peel potatoes for a Sunday roast. My arms and legs would do it just fine. 

It's just... I don't have the heart for it. The spirit for it is what's gone. When it comes to the things I actually *have* to do for work or just keeping the house clean, I just push through and do them, and my energy is exactly the same as it always was. It's just the fun things. I just don't want to do them. So no, I haven't noticed my actual energy dropping at all. It's just that heavy, gray feeling I was telling you about.
